question: Can a relational-database foundation model avoid an RDB-specific trainable encoder by retaining separate, interpretable column-wise relational aggregates and delegating label-aware feature selection to an already-pretrained single-table in-context learner?

key_findings.claim: The proposed JUICE restriction keeps every output feature attributable to exactly one original RDB column rather than mixing heterogeneous columns before labels are available to the ICL decoder.
key_findings.evidence: Definition 3.1 requires each output column z_:l to be a function of one source column t_k:j and independent of all other columns. The construction then separates column-specific subgraphs and meta-paths, applies one-dimensional aggregation, and concatenates their outputs for label-aware selection downstream.

anchors.section: 3 A Foundation for RDB Foundation Models

key_findings.claim: The paper itself identifies settings in which the argument for strict vertical-only encoding no longer applies.
key_findings.evidence: Local historical labels inside an encoder neighborhood, schema or column metadata, LLM feature selection, and text that explicitly describes a cross-column target can all give the encoder task information or justify engineered cross-column interactions; the authors defer a rigorous treatment of local-label access.

anchors.section: D Arbitrating Homophily vs Heterophily Relationships

key_findings.claim: The no-training headline means no RDB-specific encoder training or task fine-tuning, not a model trained from scratch without pretraining.
key_findings.evidence: RDBLearn pairs parameter-free SQL/feature-synthesis encodings with TabPFN v2, TabPFN v2.5, or LimiX checkpoints, each of which is a pretrained single-table ICL model. The paper's distinction is that those checkpoints never train on the inference-time RDB through the RDBLearn pipeline.

anchors.section: 3.4 Combining JUICE with a single-table ICL model

key_findings.claim: RDBLearn operationalizes JUICE approximately through parameter-free relational feature synthesis compiled to SQL rather than by literally executing the theoretical one-dimensional meta-path GNN.
key_findings.evidence: The system uses DuckDB/FeatureTools-style DFS primitives, aggregation pushdown, caching or materialization, cutoff-time constraints, and relative time differences. Appendix E says it featurizes 'following the spirit of JUICE'; Appendix F fixes continuous aggregators to sum/mean/mode/min/max/std and categorical aggregators to counts/mode.

key_findings.claim: Proposition 3.2 removes scalar weights only for a narrow one-dimensional, positive-homogeneous, nonnegative-weight, loop-free meta-path construction; it does not establish equivalence to general learned relational encoders.
key_findings.evidence: The proof relies on a special initialization in which a node is zero immediately before its sole neighbor-aggregation step, on each table being traversed at most once, and on all scalar weights being nonnegative so they can be pulled through degree-one homogeneous functions. These conditions exclude ordinary signed matrix filters, recurrent/repeated-table propagation, and multidimensional cross-column encoders.

key_findings.claim: The synthetic study supports a specific failure mode: invertible random dense mixing hurts TabPFN when added columns are uninformative, but has little effect when every added column contributes to the target.
key_findings.evidence: Across 100 independently generated datasets per point, a random linear–leaky-ReLU–linear invertible encoder shows a growing accuracy penalty as noise columns are added; the control experiment extending the target weight vector to make added columns informative reports little encoder effect. This is also a negative/null result against a blanket claim that dense mixing is always harmful.

anchors.section: 4.2 motivation and pointer to Appendix B
B Empirical Corroboration of Dense Encoder Performance Degradation, Figure 8

key_findings.claim: The exact-recovery proof for Proposition 4.2 does not justify the stated condition n>kappa.
key_findings.evidence: The proof invokes full spark and uniqueness of a sparse solution with ||w||_0<n. Sparse equality-solution uniqueness generally needs a two-sparsity condition such as 2kappa<spark(X)=n+1, not merely kappa<n; at n=kappa+1, multiple affine supports with invertible augmented designs can interpolate the n observations. The derivation also subtracts an intercept b without specifying how the fixed decoder knows or jointly identifies it.

key_findings.claim: The lower half of Proposition 4.2 is unsupported for an arbitrary r-dimensional fixed encoder.
key_findings.evidence: The proof asserts that an r-dimensional output can reconstruct at most r coordinate columns and therefore succeeds only when all informative coordinates fall in one retained subset. No continuity, finite-precision, linearity, or coordinate-selection restriction is imposed on g_phi, so output dimension alone does not imply this coordinate-counting argument for arbitrary real-valued nonlinear encoders.

key_findings.claim: The claimed O(n^-2/kappa) original-coordinate rate in Proposition 4.3 is not established for all kappa covered by the proposition statement.
key_findings.evidence: The proof obtains O(n^-2/kappa)+O(sqrt(log binomial(d,kappa)/n)) and explicitly says the first term dominates only for kappa>4. The theorem statement omits that restriction, so the displayed rate does not follow from the proof for kappa<=4.

key_findings.claim: The n^-2/d lower-bound argument in Proposition 4.3 does not match the operational claim about a fixed pretrained encoder paired with its decoder.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 13 takes an infimum over decoders against a supremum over an adversarial unknown bi-Lipschitz encoder. The proof observes that a coordinate of g_phi^-1 is Lipschitz and cites a generic d-dimensional Lipschitz minimax rate, but does not show that inverse-coordinate functions induced by the allowed bijections contain the requisite hard class or that the paired decoder lacks knowledge of its own fixed encoder.

anchors.section: G Technical Proofs, statement of Proposition G.3

key_findings.claim: Consequently, the main-text statement that dense OOD encoding can change the sample-complexity exponent from kappa to ambient dimension d should be treated as an unproven motivating hypothesis, not a demonstrated theorem.
key_findings.evidence: That interpretation depends on both parts of Proposition 4.3, whose original-coordinate upper rate has a missing kappa restriction and whose dense-encoder lower bound uses an adversarial unknown-transform formulation with an incomplete class-hardness argument.

key_findings.claim: On the retained RelBench-v1 classification tasks, RDBLearn has the best reported mean among foundation-model systems and nearly reaches the fully supervised RelGT.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 reports mean AUC 74.81 for RDBLearn versus 72.72 for KumoRFM, 70.09 for RT, 70.02 for RandGNN, and 75.34 for supervised RelGT; rel-event and rel-f1 are excluded for identified or suspected leakage. RDBLearn is reported as uniformly above the same-decoder RandGNN ablation in the displayed tasks.

key_findings.claim: RelBench-v1 comparisons are not a clean encoder-only study because baseline access, pretraining data, code availability, tuning, and regression metrics differ.
key_findings.evidence: RT, Griffin, and RelLLM reported results were pretrained on RelBench-v1 databases; KumoRFM is closed and its real-data mixture is undisclosed; most RT regression R2 results could not be reproduced; and the paper imports tuned results from original authors. RandGNN is the clearest same-backend cross-column ablation, but no uncertainty over seeds is reported.

anchors.section: A ICL and synthetic pre-training for RDB learning

key_findings.claim: The paper contradicts itself about validation-set and hyperparameter use.
key_findings.evidence: Section 6 explicitly chooses H in {2,3} and the decoder family among TabPFN v2, TabPFN v2.5, and LimiX using development sets. Figure 7 later supports the claim that the method works 'without ever touching benchmark validation sets, nor adjusting any hyperparameters across different tasks.' Stability across six settings does not erase the stated development-set selection.

key_findings.claim: The RelBench-v1 regression result is competitive rather than dominant.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 3 reports normalized mean MAE 1.074 for RDBLearn, 1.088 for KumoRFM, and 1.000 for supervised RelGT. The appendix also reports that most external RT regression R2 values could not be reproduced, leaving only the two rel-trial tasks for that comparison.

key_findings.claim: The preliminary RelBench-v2 result is positive on four of five available in-scope tasks but contains a concrete regression loss and excludes two datasets.
key_findings.evidence: RDBLearn exceeds the supervised GNN on all three displayed classification tasks (97.81/84.92/81.68 versus 94.27/78.67/80.51) and user-count MAE (7.231 versus 7.374), but loses on beer-ratings MAE (0.434 versus 0.323). rel-arxiv is excluded because it is text-heavy and rel-mimic because it was unavailable.

key_findings.claim: On 4DBInfer, RDBLearn is broadly competitive but is not the best model on most individual tasks.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports RDBLearn AUC 0.7741/0.5447/0.8469/0.8845/0.8796 on Amazon churn, Outbrain CTR, RetailRocket CVR, StackExchange post upvote, and StackExchange user churn. Supervised baselines exceed it on four tasks by varying margins, while the aggregate ranking remains strong for a no-RDB-training system.

key_findings.claim: The claimed orders-of-magnitude efficiency advantage is an indicative budget comparison, not a controlled latency benchmark.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix contrasts roughly 10^2 seconds of total RDBLearn latency on a 4080 with 10^3–10^4 seconds for one supervised run and then multiplies the latter by a 100-configuration hyperparameter sweep to obtain 10^5–10^6 seconds. Environments are acknowledged to differ, and no distribution, variance, preprocessing breakdown, or equal-search-budget comparison is given.

key_findings.claim: The reported supervised-to-ICL 'performance inversion' is suggestive but not a controlled causal ablation of encoder training.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 6 compares KumoRFM and RelGT sharing a dense encoder against RDBLearn and AutoGluon using JUICE-like features, so encoder, decoder, objective, training data, and tuning change together. Appendix C recombines published GraphPFN and G2T results with OOM omissions rather than running a new matched experiment, although the repeated qualitative pattern is useful corroboration.

anchors.section: 6 JUICE is worth the squeeze, Figure 6
C Lessons from Graph Foundation Models, Figure 9

key_findings.claim: The system's current scope omits raw text and does not solve label-aware homophily-versus-heterophily arbitration in the encoder.
key_findings.evidence: All raw, special-text, and n-gram features are disabled, and rel-arxiv is excluded. Appendix D explicitly leaves task-dependent homophily/heterophily selection as future work; adding more aggregators reportedly helped in preliminary tests, but those results are not shown.

anchors.section: D Arbitrating Homophily vs Heterophily Relationships

key_findings.claim: The practical contribution is unusually reusable even where the theory is not: it exposes a scikit-learn-compatible, leakage-aware SQL relational-featurization layer that can swap among tabular ICL backends.
key_findings.evidence: The API maps target rows to database context through key mappings, enforces per-instance cutoff times, produces fixed-length features, caches or materializes SQL intermediates, and accepts compatible base estimators. This makes the column-preserving design independently testable against stronger future tabular models.

method.core_idea: Preserve a coordinate system the label-aware tabular ICL decoder can interpret: aggregate relational information vertically within one source column and one meta-path at a time, concatenate those features, and avoid any learned horizontal cross-column encoder on a new RDB.
method.mechanism: For each target row, RDBLearn traverses PK–FK relations within H hops, computes fixed parameter-free continuous, categorical, and relative-time aggregates per source column/meta-path using SQL/FeatureTools-style primitives, concatenates them with task-table features, and conditions a pretrained TabPFN v2/v2.5 or LimiX decoder on up to 10,000 labeled training rows. H and decoder family are selected from six configurations using development data; the implementation uses one 32GB RTX 4080 and disables raw text.
assumptions: Source-column identity is stable and more useful to an OOD ICL decoder than an entangled dense representation.
The encoder lacks enough label, schema, metadata, or semantic information to choose cross-column interactions before the ICL stage.
A fixed menu of aggregates and H in {2,3} captures the relevant relational neighborhood without task-specific encoder learning.
The pretrained single-table backend can select useful dimensions and model the remaining interactions from labeled in-context examples.
Cutoff-time and PK–FK metadata are correct, and train/dev/test temporal splits prevent future-information leakage.
Theoretical weight-removal applies only under one-dimensional positive-homogeneous propagation, nonnegative scalar weights, special initialization, and non-repeating meta-paths.

The analytical OOD arguments use idealized absolutely continuous features, sparse coordinate targets, and—within Proposition 4.3—an unknown bi-Lipschitz transform; these do not directly model the evaluated RDB pipeline.

techniques.role: Constrains each encoded feature to depend on one original RDB column, retaining column identity until label-aware decoding.
Forms independent one-dimensional relational views for each source column and PK–FK meta-path.
Computes continuous sum/mean/mode/min/max/std and categorical count/mode features without RDB-specific training.
Executes joins, cutoff-time filters, aggregation, caching, and materialization in the database engine.
Uses time differences instead of absolute future timestamps to reduce temporal OOD effects.
Uses pretrained TabPFN v2/v2.5 or LimiX to select and combine relational features from labeled examples.
Tests the effect of random cross-column mixing while retaining a single-table foundation-model decoder.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic binary classification with random invertible dense encoders; 100 generated datasets per plotted point
evaluations.metric: TabPFN v2 test accuracy as informative or uninformative columns are added
evaluations.result: Dense mixing increasingly hurts when added columns are uninformative, but has little effect when the target depends on every added column.
evaluations.baseline: Original coordinate features without the random linear–leaky-ReLU–linear transform

evaluations.setting: RelBench-v1 entity classification after excluding rel-event and rel-f1
evaluations.result: RDBLearn 74.81; KumoRFM 72.72; RT 70.09; RandGNN 70.02; supervised RelGT 75.34.
evaluations.baseline: Foundation models KumoRFM, RT, Griffin, RelLLM and LLM baselines; RandGNN encoder ablation; supervised RelGT reference

evaluations.result: RDBLearn 1.074, KumoRFM 1.088, and supervised RelGT 1.000; reproducible R2 comparison against RT/Griffin is limited to two rel-trial tasks.
evaluations.baseline: KumoRFM, RandGNN, supervised RelGT, plus limited RT/Griffin rel-trial results

evaluations.setting: Preliminary RelBench-v2 binary classification and regression; rel-arxiv and rel-mimic omitted
evaluations.metric: AUROC for three classification tasks and MAE for two regression tasks
evaluations.result: RDBLearn beats the supervised GNN on all three classification tasks and user-count regression, but is worse on beer-ratings regression (0.434 versus 0.323 MAE), hence four of five tasks.
evaluations.baseline: Released supervised GNN, Griffin, and RandGNN

evaluations.setting: Five 4DBInfer classification tasks with a common RDBLearn pipeline
evaluations.result: RDBLearn obtains 0.7741, 0.5447, 0.8469, 0.8845, and 0.8796 and a strong aggregate rank, but is individually outscored by a supervised baseline on four of five tasks.
evaluations.baseline: Eight tuned heterogeneous-GNN/graph-extraction combinations, Griffin, and RandGNN

evaluations.setting: 4DBInfer indicative runtime comparison on comparable RTX 4080-class hardware
evaluations.result: RDBLearn is reported around 10^2 seconds; one supervised run is 10^3–10^4 seconds and a 100-run HPO budget is 10^5–10^6 seconds.
evaluations.baseline: Supervised 4DBInfer models with their full hyperparameter sweep

evaluations.metric: Mean AUROC across six decoder-by-H configurations
evaluations.result: TabPFN v2 scores 73.94/74.55, TabPFN v2.5 scores 72.03/74.30, and LimiX scores 73.03/73.74 for H=2/H=3, showing useful but nonzero selection sensitivity.
evaluations.baseline: Cross-comparison of the three pretrained tabular decoders and two hop counts

evaluations.setting: Cross-regime performance-inversion analysis on RDB and reused graph-foundation-model results
evaluations.metric: Difference between JUICE-like and dense-encoder performance in supervised versus ICL regimes
evaluations.result: Both plots show the hypothesized sign reversal, but the systems, training data, objectives, and OOM-complete task sets are not controlled as a single matched experiment.
evaluations.baseline: KumoRFM/RelGT versus RDBLearn/AutoGluon; GraphPFN versus G2T variants

limitations: The exact-recovery and sample-complexity propositions have material proof gaps, so they do not currently establish the strongest ambient-dimension claims.
The operational encoder is a SQL/DFS approximation 'in the spirit' of JUICE rather than a direct implementation of the analyzed one-dimensional GNN.
H and decoder family are selected using development sets despite a later statement that validation sets are never touched.
Real-benchmark tables report point estimates without seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.
Competitor comparisons mix open and closed systems, different pretraining exposure, imported tuned results, and inconsistent regression protocols.
Raw text is disabled; rel-arxiv and unavailable rel-mimic are excluded, and two RelBench-v1 tasks are excluded for leakage concerns.
The fixed aggregator menu may not express task-dependent homophily, heterophily, quantiles, entropy, or semantic cross-column rules.
Timing compares one RDBLearn pipeline with an entire 100-trial supervised HPO budget rather than equal search budgets and environments.
The 10,000-row random training downsample is a system choice whose variance and interaction with temporal data are not reported.
failure_modes: Tasks whose label is defined by a cross-column product, ratio, or semantic rule may require explicit engineered interactions that strict JUICE forbids before decoding.
Schema metadata or local historical labels can make a learned encoder's task-aware feature selection feasible, undermining the paper's encoder-information premise.
High-order relational signals beyond H=3 or path interactions that must be combined before aggregation can be lost.
Text-heavy databases are poorly served by the current implementation and may be excluded entirely.
A fixed aggregate set can blur heterophilous and homophilous effects or miss distributional shape beyond its summary statistics.
Wide relational feature synthesis can still create many distracting columns and stress the row/feature limits of the tabular ICL backend.
A future native RFM with early task information and learned noise-robust column selection can outperform parameter-free flattening, as later competitors explicitly target.
reusable_insights: When task identity arrives only with labeled context, preserve semantically stable coordinates until the label-aware stage instead of forcing an upstream task-agnostic bottleneck.
Treat parameter-free relational feature synthesis as a serious foundation-model adapter, not only as a classical baseline.
Pair every consistency or robustness claim about an encoder with a same-decoder random-mixing and identity-coordinate control.
Compile temporal cutoff constraints into query execution rather than applying them after materializing features.
Report negative controls explicitly: dense mixing was approximately neutral when all added features were informative, and RDBLearn lost the beer-ratings regression task.
Separate no downstream/RDB training from no pretraining; frozen pretrained decoders still embody substantial training.
For representation-dimension lower bounds, state regularity and information constraints explicitly; output dimension alone is not a coordinate-capacity theorem.
open_questions: Can the Proposition 4.2 lower bound be repaired under continuous/Lipschitz or finite-precision encoders, and what is the correct sample threshold for exact sparse affine support recovery with an intercept?
Can Proposition 4.3 be restated for a known fixed encoder paired with its decoder and proved for the actual inverse-coordinate function class?
Does a same-architecture, same-data, same-decoder experiment causally isolate vertical aggregation from learned cross-column encoding?
How does JUICE scale with very wide schemas, longer paths, more than 10,000 labeled rows, missing keys, and schema drift?
Can label-aware but leakage-safe metadata or local-label signals select a small set of cross-column interactions before ICL?
What uncertainty remains across database splits, random downsampling, decoder seeds, SQL execution order, and benchmark tasks?
How does RDBLearn compare under matched compute and current revisions of KumoRFM-2, OpenRFM, and Relational Transformer?
Can raw-text encoders preserve the provenance/column separability principle while serving text-centric datasets?

competitive_landscape.title: Griffin: Towards a Graph-Centric Relational Database Foundation Model
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct dense-encoder antecedent evaluated in the paper; Griffin jointly pretrains relational encoders and a task decoder on single-table and RDB data and is repeatedly used to motivate JUICE's different inductive bias
competitive_landscape.difference: Griffin uses metadata encoders, cross-attention, and trainable message passing with pretraining/fine-tuning, whereas RDBLearn freezes a pretrained tabular decoder and computes parameter-free, column-separated relational features. Its zero-shot result imported here is weaker, but the protocols are not matched.

competitive_landscape.title: Relational Transformer: Toward Zero-Shot Foundation Models for Relational Data
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct RFM competitor and experimental baseline; the paper discusses RT's task-table labels, schema metadata, and pretraining exposure as caveats to a purely task-blind encoder
competitive_landscape.difference: RT tokenizes cells with table/column metadata, uses relational attention over row/column/key structure, and pretrains via masked-token prediction for zero-shot use without retrieved ICL examples. RDBLearn instead supplies explicit labeled ICL rows to a tabular backend and does no RDB-specific pretraining.

competitive_landscape.title: Large Language Models are Good Relational Learners
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct relational-learning competitor evaluated as Rel-LLM and used in the paper's analysis of nominal zero-shot systems trained on RelBench-v1
competitive_landscape.difference: Rel-LLM encodes local temporal subgraphs with a GNN and denormalizes them into structured retrieval-augmented LLM prompts. RDBLearn uses numeric/categorical SQL aggregates and a tabular ICL decoder, avoiding both trainable relational encoding and LLM text reasoning.

competitive_landscape.title: KumoRFM-2: Scaling Foundation Models for Relational Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: later direct primary competitor to both the closed KumoRFM version evaluated in this paper and the broad claim that an RDB encoder need not be trained
competitive_landscape.difference: KumoRFM-2 natively pretrains across row, column, key, and cross-sample axes on synthetic plus real databases, injects task information early to select relevant noisy columns, supports ICL and fine-tuning, evaluates 41 benchmarks, and scales to billion-row data. It therefore targets precisely the task-blindness and scale limitations used to justify JUICE.

competitive_landscape.title: OpenRFM: Dissecting Relational In-Context Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: later direct open RFM competitor that analyzes sparse relational ICL and improves the RT backbone with a tabular ICL stage
competitive_landscape.difference: OpenRFM combines a learned relational backbone with a pretrained batch-level tabular ICL layer and homophily-aware synthetic plus continual-real pretraining, reporting roughly 30% average improvement over RT and surpassing KumoRFMv1. Unlike RDBLearn, it retains learned cross-column relational representations while addressing label scarcity explicitly.

competitive_landscape.title: PluRel: Synthetic Data unlocks Scaling Laws for Relational Foundation Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: contemporaneous primary evidence for the alternative strategy of training relational foundation models on diverse synthetic databases
competitive_landscape.difference: PluRel generates schemas, PK–FK connectivity, and conditional feature distributions and reports power-law pretraining scaling plus better real-database generalization as synthetic database count grows. RDBLearn avoids relational pretraining and instead depends on a fixed human-designed aggregation basis; PluRel supplies evidence that continued RFM training can be productive rather than categorically unnecessary.

competitive_landscape.title: RelBench v2: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Repository for Relational Data
competitive_landscape.relationship: primary benchmark source used for the paper's preliminary new-domain experiments and for its RandGNN implementation
competitive_landscape.difference: RelBench v2 spans 11 datasets, over 22 million rows, 29 tables, autocomplete/forecasting/recommendation tasks, and reports relational models consistently beating single-table baselines. The present paper evaluates only the available non-text subset and therefore does not yet establish coverage of the full v2 scope.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first principled case that an ICL-oriented RDB encoder should preserve column identity, that trainable parameters can be removed from this encoder family without appreciable expressiveness loss, and that dense OOD encoders can worsen exact recovery or sample complexity; RDBLearn is presented as an open, scalable SQL realization that outperforms prior RDB foundation models without RDB training or fine-tuning.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The strongest evidence is empirical: a clear JUICE definition, an open swappable SQL pipeline, a same-backend RandGNN comparison, broad RelBench/4DBInfer coverage, a synthetic informative-versus-noise control, and competitive point estimates including 74.81 mean RelBench-v1 AUC. Proposition 3.2 is valid only for its restricted scalar construction, while the Appendix G proofs of Propositions 4.2 and 4.3 do not establish their full statements.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The practical composition—column-provenance-preserving relational feature synthesis plus modern tabular ICL—is novel, useful, and well supported as a strong baseline. The wider claims that encoder training is generally unnecessary and that dense encoders provably incur ambient-dimension sample complexity are overstated: later task-aware RFMs are direct counterevidence, comparisons are not fully controlled, and the key theoretical lower bounds contain substantive gaps.

reviewer_notes: Reviewed the complete current target revision arXiv:2602.13697v2 from the indexed 22-page PDF, including every main-text page, reference pages 10–13, and Appendices A–G on pages 14–22. Appendix G equations and proof logic were checked against the rendered PDF, including the inf–sup order in Equation 13 and the kappa>4 qualification following Equation 19. Figure/table values were transcribed from the PDF, and negative/null outcomes were retained rather than collapsed into the headline: informative-column mixing was approximately neutral, RDBLearn lost one RelBench-v2 regression task, and it was not individually best on most 4DBInfer tasks. Source provenance is copied exactly from the fulltext index. Seven primary competitors/benchmark sources were checked on official arXiv records current on 2026-08-23 and pinned to exact revisions. Confidence is high on the empirical extraction and stated protocol, and calibrated below certainty because some imported/closed baseline results are not independently reproducible and the theorem critique identifies proof gaps rather than supplying complete replacement theorems.
